rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding argument invokes signs within human beings and in the external world; the ensuing passage makes the unseen punishment vivid to the deniers.
rows.anchor: through the signs found in the world inside man and those found outside him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage portrays what is still unseen as before the deniers and orders them toward what they denied, staging the threat as an immediate scene.
rows.anchor: what at the moment eludes the eyes, is portrayed before these disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shadow is the shade cast by smoke, rather than an ordinary protective shadow.
rows.anchor: here obviously it does not refer to the conventional shadow but to the shadow cast by smoke

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi supports the smoky shade reading with al-Wāqiʿah's description of pitch-black smoke that is neither cool nor refreshing.
rows.anchor: the shade of pitch-black smoke, neither cool nor refreshing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three-branched smoke spreads around the deniers; the direction from which they are driven is temporarily safe, but smoke engulfs them beyond it.
rows.anchor: A characteristic of the shadow mentioned here is that it will have three branches.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some interpret the three branches as punishments corresponding to indifference to God, indifference to creation, and denial of resurrection; Islahi rejects this as unsupported and far-fetched.
rows.anchor: some people have raised the point that disbelief has three characteristics

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers the straightforward spatial reading: with one of four directions secure, smoke surrounds the deniers from the other three.
rows.anchor: three directions remain, and all these will be embraced by smoke

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The smoky shadow gives the deniers no protection; it contains smoke's harmful features and none of its useful, cooling effects.
rows.anchor: The shadow will not protect them in any way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it” refers to the fire, omitted because smoke necessarily implies the fire's presence.
rows.anchor: is the fire, which is suppressed because of the mention of smoke

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some readers differ over the recitation and interpretation of the word for the sparks, though the passage does not specify their alternatives.
rows.anchor: Some people have differed in the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi follows the mutawātir reading and understands the word as “a castle” or “a dome.”
rows.anchor: hence the word means “a castle” or “a dome.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The castle or dome simile presents the flames' expanse, height, and color, with elevated, distant-shining tops distinct in color from their bases.
rows.anchor: It is a very powerful comparison of the flames which arise from a large fire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the next verse refers back to the sparks or flames just described.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the pronoun in the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective “ṣufr” can be singular or plural and masculine or feminine; here it is plural, matching the plural comparison.
rows.anchor: Here it is in the plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Jimalāt” denotes a herd of camels.
rows.anchor: is used for a herd of camels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel comparison conveys the flames' size and color; smoke makes their color a faded yellow.
rows.anchor: This comparison reflects both the colour and size of the flames.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated threat follows naturally because witnessing this horrifying scene brings destruction upon those who denied the Day.
rows.anchor: This verse is followed by the recurrent verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After depicting the Day's horror, the passage turns to the criminals' helplessness: none can speak or offer excuses, unlike their eloquent denials in worldly life.
rows.anchor: After a portrayal of the horror of the Day of Judgement, the helplessness of the criminals is depicted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The criminals' mouths will be sealed and their limbs will testify to their crimes; they neither dare speak nor may present an excuse.
rows.anchor: the mouths of the criminals will be sealed and the Almighty will give power of speech to their limbs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nabaʾ is the counterpart sūrah and gives the parallel statement that no one has authority to speak on God's behalf.
rows.anchor: the counterpart of this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain follows because the criminals cannot initiate speech or receive permission to make excuses, leaving only devastation in store.
rows.anchor: when they will neither even be able to take the initiative in speaking nor will they be granted permission to present any excuse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address answers mockery about whether ancestors will be resurrected: God declares that the deniers and all earlier peoples have been gathered, then challenges them to act.
rows.anchor: By this sarcastic question, their intention was to prove that the Day of Judgement was the most impossible of events

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge invites former plotters to try any remaining scheme against God, with their clan and all earlier and later people available to help if they can.
rows.anchor: if they now have any scheme left, they should test it too; they have with them all the people of their clan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān calls the deniers' efforts to defeat their messenger “plot.”
rows.anchor: to deny their messenger are called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says these efforts protect the leaders' position: despite knowing the Prophet's truth, ego blocks admission, so they invent objections to mislead people and defend ancestral religion.
rows.anchor: The reason for using this word is that all these efforts on their part were

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated threat follows because the deniers will be helpless before God's demand and will be utterly routed for their denial.
rows.anchor: their helplessness before the demand of God referred to earlier will become evident to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from criminals' all-encompassing punishment to the righteous, whose shade, springs, and desired fruits surround them on every side.
rows.anchor: the purpose is to bring to light the fact that these blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This way of describing blessings as surrounding the righteous appears elsewhere in the Qurʾān and has examples in classical Arabic poetry.
rows.anchor: several examples of it in classical Arabic poetry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous receive soothing, pure food and drink as reward; their worldly provisions benefit them because they fulfilled their duties, while the ingrates' provisions become useless and destructive.
rows.anchor: Eating and drinking will be soothing to them and the food and drinks will be absolutely pure and unadulterated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word describing the reward means that it is beneficial and advantageous.
rows.anchor: means “to be beneficial and advantageous.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is an accusative of state whose described noun is understood from the preceding verb.
rows.anchor: It is an accusative of state from the object evident from the previous verb.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Nisāʾ 4:4, the described noun is explicit; this illustrates the common construction of a circumstantial accusative from its described noun, like the cited phrase about a traveler.
rows.anchor: accusative of state to occur from a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse contrasts God's reward of the well-doers with the earlier statement that He deals with criminals in this way.
rows.anchor: This verse points to verse 18 above whose words are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain contrasts the righteous' eternal bliss with the deniers' severe punishment; worldly pleasure-seekers will recognize their wretched fate when they see the two outcomes.
rows.anchor: on the one hand, the righteous shall be in eternal bliss and, on the other, the disbelievers shall be subject to severe punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse now directly addresses Quraysh's leaders, warning them that worldly luxuries are transient and do not promise comfort in the Hereafter; only righteousness would avail them.
rows.anchor: Here at the end, the leaders of the Quraysh are addressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain warns that the deniers face devastation beyond anything imaginable in worldly life.
rows.anchor: The placement and occasion of the recurrent verse are clear:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address becomes indirect: when asked to kneel before God in gratitude for His favors, the arrogant refuse, despite their assumption that worldly comforts secure Hereafter comforts.
rows.anchor: they do not comply; on the contrary, they express arrogance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kneeling refers to prayer, the greatest expression of gratitude to God and the greatest destroyer of arrogance and pride.
rows.anchor: the greatest manifestation of showing gratitude to the Almighty and the greatest destroyer of arrogance and pride.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qalam describes the deniers being called to prostrate on Judgment Day but unable, since they did not prostrate in worldly life; this confirms their arrogance and their deserved punishment.
rows.anchor: when on the Day of Judgement these disbelievers will be called to prostrate before the Almighty, they will not be able to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain warns haughty people who neglect their obligations yet demand their rights that their desires will not be fulfilled.
rows.anchor: the megalomaniacs and the haughty who are not ready to carry out their obligations and yet want their rights to be fulfilled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final question rebukes the deniers' stubbornness: nothing is more persuasive than the Qurʾān, and the Prophet is assured that reason will not cure their refusal; belief after seeing the truth will be too late.
rows.anchor: then what else will they profess faith in?

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: An alternative reading asks what they will believe in after the Day arrives; everyone will then believe, but that belief will be useless.
rows.anchor: after the advent of this day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi considers both readings possible but prefers the more comprehensive question of what could surpass God's revelations as proof, citing al-Jāthiyah 45:6.
rows.anchor: Although both these interpretations are correct and the purport of the verses is not much different in either, however, my interpretation seems more comprehensive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbasa pairs with al-Nāziʿāt and shares its central theme, discourse style, and reasoning; the changed sequence of topics gives this sūrah its distinct majesty.
rows.anchor: There is no basic difference between the central theme of both sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nāziʿāt ends by calling the Prophet a warner for those who fear Judgment; ʿAbasa opens by rebuking him for attending to arrogant Quraysh leaders who demand the poor companions be turned away.
rows.anchor: you are but a warner for people who fear it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet is addressed in the rebuke, its intended target is the haughty leaders who ignore his message and want poor companions excluded to secure their own attendance.
rows.anchor: Although the Prophet (sws) is addressed, yet the direction of this stern address is towards these supercilious people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's responsibility is to teach those who come eagerly, including devoted companions, rather than pamper absent leaders; he is not accountable for those who refuse to come.
rows.anchor: His real responsibility is to educate and instruct only those who come to him enthusiastically.
